paragraphs: The rain lashed against the leaded glass windows of Harrington Manor, each gust of wind a mournful howl that seemed to echo through the cavernous library. Inside, the only sound was the crackle of the hearth and the quiet, steady ticking of the grandfather clock in the hall. It was this unnerving silence that Arthur Penwright, the family’s butler of thirty years, found most disturbing. He pushed open the heavy oak door to find his employer, Lord Alistair Harrington, slumped in his high-backed leather chair, a silver letter opener protruding from the starched white of his shirt. A half-empty glass of amber liquid lay shattered on the Persian rug, its contents mingling with a growing crimson stain.

Detective Inspector Davies arrived less than an hour later, his trench coat dripping onto the pristine marble of the foyer. A man whose weary eyes had seen too many such scenes, he surveyed the library with a practiced calm that contrasted sharply with the butler's trembling hands. Davies knelt beside the body, careful not to disturb anything, his gaze lingering not on the wound, but on a small, muddy scuff mark near the leg of the mahogany desk, a detail oddly out of place in the meticulously kept room.

In the drawing room, Davies found the rest of the household gathered in a tense tableau. Lady Eleanor Harrington sat bolt upright in a wingback chair, her face a mask of porcelain grief, her hands clasped so tightly in her lap that her knuckles were white. Pacing before the unlit fireplace was Julian Croft, Lord Harrington’s fiery-tempered nephew, his handsome face contorted with an emotion that looked more like fury than sorrow. Observing them both from a distance was Dr. Alistair Finch, the family physician, a quiet, unassuming man whose presence seemed almost an afterthought.

"My condolences, Lady Harrington," Davies began, his voice a soft rumble. "Can you tell me when you last saw your husband alive?" Eleanor's gaze was distant, fixed on a point beyond the rain-streaked window. "He retired to the library after dinner, as was his custom. He said he had some papers to review." She paused, dabbing a lace handkerchief at the corner of her eye, a gesture that seemed more practiced than heartfelt. "I heard shouting a short while later. It was Julian. He was demanding money again, and Alistair… Alistair was finally refusing him. He threatened to write him out of the will entirely."

Davies turned his gaze, which had all the warmth of a winter sea, to the pacing nephew. "Mr. Croft. Your aunt mentioned an argument concerning money and the will." Julian scoffed, running a hand through his disheveled hair. "Of course we argued! He was a cantankerous old goat who delighted in holding his fortune over my head. I told him he couldn't control me forever." He stopped abruptly, his jaw tight. "But I didn't kill him. I may have been furious, but I'm not a murderer. I just… needed to get some air."

"And you, Doctor?" Davies's attention shifted to the quiet physician. "What brought you to the manor on such a foul evening?" Dr. Finch adjusted his spectacles, his expression unreadable. "Lord Harrington summoned me. He'd been complaining of some chest pains earlier. I was waiting in the hall for him to conclude his business with his nephew." He gestured vaguely in Julian's direction. "The shouting was... quite pronounced. I thought it best not to intrude." Davies’s eyes flicked down, noting the doctor’s impeccably clean shoes before they settled on Julian's. The younger man’s brogues were indeed damp, with small, tell-tale specks of mud clinging to the welts, a perfect match for the mark in the library.

Inspector Davies turned back to the butler, who had been standing silently by the doorway, a ghost in his own home. "Mr. Penwright, you discovered the body. Tell me precisely what you observed after the argument." The butler swallowed, his Adam's apple bobbing. "I heard the shouting cease, sir, followed by the library door slamming shut. A moment later, I saw Mr. Croft storming down the west wing corridor. He looked… well, he looked enraged. He didn’t seem to see me at all as he went straight out the side door into the garden. It was perhaps five minutes later that I entered the library to check on his Lordship."

Davies's eyes narrowed on Julian Croft, who had stopped his pacing and was now watching the interrogation with a defiant sneer. "You went out into the garden, you said? In this downpour?" Davies's voice was deceptively mild. "It seems a rather odd time for a constitutional. You stormed out of the library, slammed the door, and went straight outside, just moments before your uncle was found dead. It paints a rather incriminating picture, wouldn't you agree, Mr. Croft?" The accusation hung in the air, thick and heavy as the scent of wet wool and old books.

A bitter laugh escaped Julian’s lips, a sound utterly devoid of mirth. "Oh, this is rich. Yes, I was angry. Yes, I went outside to keep from putting my fist through a priceless Ming vase. And yes, my shoes are muddy. It’s a garden, Inspector, it tends to get muddy in a bloody downpour." He took a half-step towards the detective, his voice dropping to a low, challenging growl. "You think I’d be stupid enough to stab the old man and then traipse mud all over the crime scene? I wanted his money, not his life. A dead man can't sign a cheque, Inspector."

Unfazed by the outburst, Davies redirected his attention to Lady Eleanor, whose composure remained impeccable, almost unnaturally so. "Lady Harrington, your husband's business… was it going well? Were there any recent pressures or concerns that he mentioned to you?" She delicately smoothed a non-existent wrinkle in her silk dress. "Alistair was always meticulous. The Harrington shipping line is a legacy, Inspector. It is… was… an empire. Of course, there are always rivals, but he never spoke of any specific threats. He kept his business affairs very private." Her words were precise, yet revealed nothing, like a beautifully crafted but empty porcelain vase.

Davies excused himself and returned to the silence of the library, the scent of leather and old paper now tainted with something metallic and grim. He circled the large mahogany desk, his eyes scanning the surface. Amidst a neat stack of shipping ledgers was a single sheet of foolscap, penned in Lord Harrington’s precise, spidery script. It was a hastily drafted codicil to his will, the ink barely dry. With a gloved hand, Davies read the damning words: "…and to my nephew, Julian Croft, for his continued insolence and profligate nature, I hereby bequeath nothing, revoking all previous entitlements." The document was dated that very evening.

Returning to the drawing room, Davies held the codicil aloft. "Mr. Croft, I believe this is what your argument was truly about." He read the lines aloud, his voice flat and devoid of emotion. "Your uncle was in the process of disinheriting you completely. You saw this, didn't you? You knew that once he signed it, your life of leisure was over. A powerful motive for a man of your... temper." The color drained from Julian's face, his earlier bravado crumbling into a shocked, ashen disbelief. He stared at the paper as if it were a venomous snake.

"He… he wouldn't," Julian stammered, shaking his head. "He always threatened, but he never would have gone through with it. It was a game to him, a way to keep me under his thumb." He looked around the room, his eyes wild and pleading, but found no sympathy. Lady Eleanor simply stared into the cold hearth, and Dr. Finch polished his glasses with a slow, deliberate motion, his expression carefully neutral. Even Penwright, the butler, averted his gaze. The weight of the evidence, circumstantial though it was, seemed to press down on Julian, suffocating him.

"Perhaps we should search Mr. Croft's room," Davies suggested, the question a mere formality. He gestured to a uniformed constable who had been waiting by the door. As the constable and a reluctant Julian headed for the grand staircase, Davies took the opportunity to speak with Dr. Finch alone. "Doctor, you said Lord Harrington complained of chest pains. Was this a recurring issue?" The physician nodded slowly. "His heart was not what it used to be. The strain of running his empire was taking its toll. I had prescribed him some new medication, a potent vasodilator, just last week."

The constable returned a short while later, holding a damp tweed jacket by the collar, pinched between his thumb and forefinger. "Found this shoved in the back of the wardrobe, sir," he announced. "Still wet from the rain." Davies took the jacket and examined it carefully. There, on the right cuff, was a small, dark smear that was undeniably blood. It wasn't much, but combined with the motive, the argument, the muddy shoes, and the flight from the room, it formed a chain of evidence that felt cold and solid as iron.

"It's not what it looks like!" Julian protested, his voice strained with panic as he saw the jacket. "I cut myself, in the garden! I stumbled near the rose bushes, the thorns are vicious." He held up his left hand, showing a fresh, shallow scratch on his palm. "The blood must have transferred when I took the jacket off." It was a plausible explanation, yet it sounded feeble and desperate in the face of the mounting evidence against him. The noose of suspicion was tightening, and every word he spoke only seemed to pull it closer.

Davies ignored Julian's frantic explanation for the moment, his mind working through the sequence of events. The loud argument, the slamming door, Julian storming out. It was all so theatrical, so overt. He turned his attention back to Lady Eleanor, who had remained a pillar of stoic grace throughout the ordeal. "Lady Harrington," he said, his tone gentle, "I understand this is difficult, but did your husband have any enemies in his business dealings? Anyone who might have wished him harm?"

For the first time, a flicker of something unreadable crossed Lady Eleanor's face before it was smoothed away. "Alistair was a powerful man, Inspector. Powerful men make enemies." She paused, her gaze drifting towards the portrait of her late husband that hung above the mantelpiece. "There was... a recent acquisition. A smaller, rival shipping firm run by a rather unscrupulous character. Alistair drove a hard bargain, and the man lost everything. He made some rather public threats, I believe." The information was delivered with a studied nonchalance, a perfectly placed piece of misdirection.

Davies filed the information away, though his gut told him it was a dead end. The murder felt personal, contained within the suffocating walls of the manor. He looked from Julian's panicked face to Lady Eleanor's serene mask, and finally to Dr. Finch, who was quietly observing the proceedings from his corner. An idea, faint and unformed, began to prickle at the back of the inspector's mind. He walked back over to the physician. "Doctor, this medication you prescribed for Lord Harrington... what were its effects?"

Dr. Finch adjusted his spectacles, a nervous habit Davies had noted earlier. "As I said, a vasodilator. It relaxes the blood vessels, increases blood flow, and lowers blood pressure. It's quite effective for angina." He paused, choosing his next words carefully. "However, it has certain... side effects. In high doses, or when mixed with alcohol, it can cause confusion, dizziness, and a significant anticoagulant effect. It thins the blood, you see. Makes it much harder to clot." The doctor's eyes flicked for a fraction of a second towards the shattered glass on the library floor.

The shattered glass. The spilled whisky. The anticoagulant effect. The pieces clicked into place in Davies's mind, forming a picture entirely different from the one he'd been so carefully led to paint. The wound from the letter opener was precise, but not particularly deep. It might not have been fatal on its own. But with blood that refused to clot… Davies looked at the small stain on Julian's cuff, then at the much larger pool on the library floor. The volume was all wrong. He turned to face the room, his gaze settling not on the nephew, but on the quiet, unassuming man in the corner. "Dr. Finch," he said, his voice ringing with sudden authority, "Your shoes are perfectly clean. Tell me, did you by any chance change them when you arrived this evening?"

A hush fell over the room. Dr. Finch’s composure finally fractured, a fine web of cracks appearing on his placid facade. "I… I don't see the relevance," he stammered, his hand instinctively going to his medical bag which sat on a small table beside him. "The rain was quite heavy. I always keep a spare pair of shoes in my car for house calls." But the lie was thin, and his eyes betrayed a sudden, cornered fear. Everyone else had tracked in some measure of dampness, but the doctor looked as if he'd been transported directly from his surgery into the drawing room, a feat impossible on such a night.

"The argument was a wonderful distraction, wasn't it?" Davies continued, his voice relentless as he took a step towards the doctor. "You heard Julian shouting, knew he was about to storm out. You had already administered a massive dose of your 'medication' into Lord Harrington’s evening whisky, knowing it would amplify the bleeding. After Julian left, you entered the library, didn't you? Your own patient was likely confused, dizzy from the drug. It would have been easy to grab the letter opener and plunge it into his chest. Not a deep wound, just enough. The drug did the rest."

"It wasn't me! It was Julian, you have the proof!" Finch’s voice was high and reedy, a stark contrast to his earlier calm. But Davies was undeterred. "The mud scuff by the desk wasn't from Julian entering; it was from you, Doctor, when you stumbled back in surprise after the deed was done. You quickly left, went to your car to change your muddy shoes for the clean pair in your bag, and then waited in the hall to be 'found', the concerned physician. You counted on Julian's temper and his very public fight to provide the perfect cover. But you didn't count on the sheer volume of blood your anticoagulant would produce, a detail inconsistent with the small cut on Mr. Croft's hand."

Dr. Finch crumpled, his face a mask of despair and fury. "He deserved it!" he hissed, the words venomous. "For years, I tended to his every ailment, while he used my research, my medical patents, and folded them into his own soulless corporations, leaving me with scraps. He ruined me quietly, politely, over two decades. Tonight, he told me he was selling the last of the patents—my life's work—to a foreign competitor. He laughed about it." He looked at his trembling hands, the same hands that had sworn an oath to do no harm. "His heart was failing, you see. I just… gave it a little help." The confession, stark and chilling, hung in the silent room as the rain continued to beat its relentless rhythm against the dark, unforgiving windows of Harrington Manor.

first_paras: For a moment, Arthur stood frozen, the years of prim decorum a fragile dam against a tide of horror. Then, his training took over. He backed away slowly, his hand reaching for the telephone on the hall table with a tremor he hadn't felt since the Great War. An hour later, the oppressive silence of Harrington Manor was shattered by the sharp commands of constables and the flash of camera bulbs. Detective Inspector Miles Corbin, his trench coat still glistening with rain, surveyed the scene with a weary but sharp gaze. His eyes moved from the victim to the weapon, then to the spilled drink and the pool of blood. This, Corbin thought grimly, was not the work of a common burglar. This was an act of passion, executed with an item that belonged right here in this room.

For a moment, Arthur stood frozen, the years of disciplined service warring with the raw horror before him. His training won out. With a hand that trembled only slightly, he backed out of the room, closing the door softly as if not to disturb the dead further. He proceeded with measured steps up the grand staircase to Lady Eleanor Harrington's private sitting room. He found her embroidering by the fire, her needle moving with a serene, almost hypnotic rhythm. When he delivered the dreadful news, her hands stilled, but her gaze, when it met his, was as cool and clear as the winter sky.

For a moment that stretched into an eternity, Arthur’s training and composure deserted him. He took a staggering step back, his mind refusing to process the scene. Then, instinct took over. He rushed to the grand mahogany desk, his hand reaching for the telephone to summon the police and the family physician, Dr. Finch. As his fingers trembled over the receiver, a floorboard creaked in the hall. Arthur froze, his heart hammering against his ribs, suddenly and acutely aware that he was not alone in the house, and that the killer might still be lurking nearby.

A strangled gasp escaped Arthur's lips, a sound swallowed by the opulent room. His training, ingrained over decades, warred with a primal urge to flee, but he held his ground, backing away slowly from the macabre tableau. As he turned, a figure appeared in the archway, her form a pale silhouette against the darkened hall. It was Lady Eleanor Harrington, her silk robe clutched tightly at her throat. "Arthur?" she asked, her voice a fragile thread of sound. "I heard a crash. Is everything..." Her words trailed off as her eyes adjusted to the dim light, fixing upon the slumped form of her husband. A single, perfectly manicured hand flew to her mouth, stifling a cry that was more shock than sorrow.

For a moment that stretched into an eternity, Arthur remained frozen, his hand still on the cold brass of the doorknob. Then, his training kicked in, a lifetime of service overriding the horror. He backed away slowly, closing the door with a soft click before turning and striding briskly down the hall. His voice, when he found it, was a strained but steady call for Lady Eleanor. Within minutes, the household was awake, a flurry of panicked whispers and wide eyes. Lady Eleanor Harrington swept into the hall, a vision in a silk dressing gown, her face a pale, unreadable mask. Behind her trailed Julian Croft, her nephew, his youthful face flushed with a mixture of confusion and an emotion that looked unsettlingly like anger.

Detective Inspector Davies arrived less than an hour later, his trench coat dripping onto the pristine marble of the foyer. A man whose weary eyes had seen too many such scenes, he surveyed the library with a practiced calm that contrasted sharply with the butler's trembling hands. Davies knelt beside the body, careful not to disturb anything, his gaze lingering not on the wound, but on a small, muddy scuff mark near the leg of the mahogany desk, a detail oddly out of place in the meticulously kept room.

Davies addressed Lady Eleanor first, his voice gentle but firm. "My condolences, Lady Harrington. Can you tell me when you last saw your husband alive?" Her gaze flickered towards Julian before settling on the detective. "This evening, after dinner," she said, her voice barely a whisper. "He and Julian... they had a disagreement. A rather heated one. About Julian's debts, again. Alistair told him he was cut off for good. Julian stormed out, shouting... shouting dreadful things." She finally allowed a single, perfect tear to trace a path down her cheek.

"My condolences for your loss," Davies began, his voice a low rumble that commanded attention. "I must ask, was Lord Harrington expecting any trouble? Had there been any recent... disagreements?" The question hung in the air, thick with unspoken accusations. It was Lady Eleanor who broke the silence, her voice a fragile whisper, yet every word was a steel dart aimed at her nephew. "Alistair had a dreadful argument with Julian only this afternoon. It was about his debts, again. The shouting was simply terrible." Instantly, three pairs of eyes—the Inspector's, the doctor's, and her own—settled on Julian Croft, whose face darkened with a defiant scowl.

Detective Davies began with the widow, his voice a low, respectful murmur. "Lady Harrington, can you tell me where you were this evening?" She flinched, as if the question itself were an accusation, but her voice was steady when she answered. "I was in my chambers, Inspector. A headache… I was trying to rest." She paused, dabbing a lace handkerchief at the corner of her eye. "The last I saw Alistair, he was arguing with Julian. It was dreadful… so much shouting about money. I couldn’t bear to listen."

Davies's attention settled first on Julian Croft. "Mr. Croft," he began, his voice calm but firm, "I understand you had a rather heated discussion with your uncle earlier this evening." Julian stopped his pacing abruptly, his head snapping towards the detective. "Heard that from the staff, did you? Yes, we argued. The old fool was cutting me off, threatening to write me out of his will entirely. He said I was a disgrace to the Harrington name." He gestured dismissively towards the library. "But I didn't kill him. I went for a walk in the gardens to cool off, damn the rain."

"My condolences for your loss," Davies began, his voice a low, even tone that cut through the tension. "I must ask, when was the last time any of you saw Lord Harrington alive?" It was Julian Croft who answered, his pacing coming to an abrupt halt. "I saw him an hour ago," he declared, a defiant glint in his eye. "We had a row. A blasted, furious row. The old man was threatening to change his will, to cut me out completely. I told him he'd regret it." The admission, raw and unapologetic, hung in the silent room.

Eleanor's gaze was distant, fixed on a point beyond the rain-streaked window. "He retired to the library after dinner, as was his custom. He said he had some papers to review." She paused, dabbing a lace handkerchief at the corner of her eye, a gesture that seemed more practiced than heartfelt. "I heard shouting a short while later. It was Julian. He was demanding money again, and Alistair… Alistair was finally refusing him. He threatened to write him out of the will entirely."

Davies's gaze flickered to Julian's expensive brogues; they were impeccably clean, showing no sign of a trek outdoors. "The garden, Mr. Croft? In this weather?" Before Julian could form a reply, Davies turned his attention to the physician. "Dr. Finch. You were here during this exchange?" The doctor adjusted his spectacles with a steady hand. "I was. I had come to check on Alistair's blood pressure. The argument was... heated. After Julian stormed out through the French doors into the garden, Alistair clutched his chest. I was concerned, so I stayed for a few minutes to ensure he was calm before I left."

Davies's attention shifted to the quiet man by the window. "And you, Dr. Finch? What time did you arrive?" The doctor adjusted his spectacles, his expression one of professional concern. "I arrived shortly after nine. Lord Harrington had been complaining of palpitations. I came to the library door just as the argument was ending. I heard Julian shout something about being 'finished' with his uncle, and then he stormed out, nearly knocking me over. He went straight out the front door into the garden. I thought it best to give Lord Harrington a few minutes to cool down before I entered."

Davies’s gaze moved to the quiet doctor, who had remained silent in his corner. "Dr. Finch. You were present for this... disagreement?" The physician adjusted his spectacles, his expression one of professional concern. "I was, Inspector. I'd come to check on Lord Harrington's blood pressure. The argument was most unfortunate. After the shouting reached its peak, I saw Julian burst from the library and head through the conservatory doors into the garden, despite the downpour. He seemed utterly beside himself with rage."

"Get some air? In this downpour, Mr. Croft?" Davies's tone was deceptively mild. Julian faltered for a moment, his bluster evaporating. "I... yes. I walked in the gardens. I have a temper, Inspector, and the old man knew just how to stoke it. I needed to cool off." The detective's eyes flicked down to the polished leather of Julian's shoes, which looked remarkably clean, almost as if they had been recently wiped.

The Inspector's gaze then fell upon the doctor, who had remained silent throughout the exchange. "And you, Dr. Finch? You were here as well?" The physician adjusted his spectacles, his expression one of professional concern. "I was. I came to check on Alistair's blood pressure; he'd been feeling unwell. I was in the foyer when I heard the shouting. I saw young Julian storm out of the library and straight out the front door, looking absolutely incensed. He didn't even bother with a coat."

"And you, Doctor?" Davies's attention shifted to the quiet physician. "What brought you to the manor on such a foul evening?" Dr. Finch adjusted his spectacles, his expression unreadable. "Lord Harrington summoned me. He'd been complaining of some chest pains earlier. I was waiting in the hall for him to conclude his business with his nephew." He gestured vaguely in Julian's direction. "The shouting was... quite pronounced. I thought it best not to intrude." Davies’s eyes flicked down, noting the doctor’s impeccably clean shoes before they settled on Julian's. The younger man’s brogues were indeed damp, with small, tell-tale specks of mud clinging to the welts, a perfect match for the mark in the library.

Davies returned to the library, the scent of old paper and whiskey hanging heavy in the air. He moved to the grand mahogany desk where Lord Harrington had met his end. Papers were scattered across the leather top, some bearing the victim's spidery signature. Pushed to one side, almost as an afterthought, was a single sheet of foolscap, a hastily scrawled document. It was a codicil to Lord Harrington’s will, dated that very evening. In uncompromising ink, it stated that his nephew, Julian Croft, was to be disinherited entirely, with his share of the fortune to be redirected to a local charity. The motive was now written in black and white, lying right next to the murder weapon's empty sheath.

"A walk in the garden, you say, Mr. Croft?" Davies's voice was deceptively mild. He gestured for a constable to step forward. "To cool your temper, I presume? In the middle of a torrential downpour?" Julian glared, but a flicker of uncertainty crossed his face. "I... yes. I wasn't thinking clearly." The constable presented a small, clear bag to the Inspector. Inside, nestled on a white card, was a single gold cufflink, tarnished with a smear of mud. Davies held it up. "My man found this beneath the library window, half-trodden into the flowerbed. It bears the Harrington crest. I believe it matches the one currently on your right shirt cuff."

"The side door into the garden?" Davies repeated, a flicker of interest in his eyes. He motioned for a uniformed constable. "Have a look outside that door. See where the footprints lead." He then turned his attention back to the assembled suspects. "Mr. Croft, you claim you went for air. Did anyone see you? Did you speak to anyone?" Julian shook his head, a muscle twitching in his cheek. "No. I just walked. Through the rose garden, down to the old gazebo. I needed to clear my head. Is that a crime now?"

"And the side door," Davies mused aloud, his gaze turning inward. "That would lead out to the east terrace and the rose garden, wouldn't it?" The butler confirmed with a nod. "Yes, Inspector. The path there is quite muddy after a storm like this one." The pieces were locking into place with an almost audible click: a furious argument over inheritance, a threat overheard, a man storming out into the muddy garden, and a tell-tale muddy print left by the scene of the crime. Julian Croft was looking more like the culprit with every passing minute.

"So, you went into the garden, Mr. Croft?" Davies asked, his tone deceptively casual. "In this weather?" Julian shot a resentful glare at the butler, then back at the inspector. "Yes. I was incensed. I needed to walk it off, to feel the cold rain on my face. Is that a crime now, too? I walked the length of the rose garden and back. By the time I returned, the house was in an uproar." His explanation, meant to sound reasonable, only served to paint a clearer picture: a man, consumed by rage, storming out of the very room where his uncle lay dying, his muddy feet leaving the only tangible clue behind.

Davies's voice was deceptively mild. "It seems a rather odd time for a constitutional. You stormed out of the library, slammed the door, and went straight outside, just moments before your uncle was found dead. It paints a rather incriminating picture, wouldn't you agree, Mr. Croft?" The accusation hung in the air, thick and heavy as the scent of wet wool and old books.

Davies let the tension simmer for a moment before turning his attention to Lady Eleanor. "Your Ladyship, you mentioned your husband was reviewing papers. Do you know what they were?" Her gaze flickered, a momentary loss of composure before the mask of grief slipped back into place. "I… I believe they pertained to the estate. He mentioned a new codicil to his will just this morning. He was being very secretive about it." Her eyes darted towards her nephew, a subtle but unmistakable indictment. "He was determined to put his affairs in order."

Davies let the outburst hang in the air for a moment before turning his attention back to Lady Eleanor. "Your Ladyship, was your husband in good health, aside from the chest pains Dr. Finch mentioned?" Her eyes, for the first time, flickered with an unreadable emotion. "He was... robust for his age. A strong constitution." She paused, her gaze dropping to her tightly clasped hands. "However, he had been growing increasingly paranoid of late. He’d taken to locking the library door while he worked, a new habit. He was convinced someone was trying to steal his research papers."

While Julian's bluster was convincing, Davies had learned long ago not to trust displays of emotion. He requested to see Croft's room. Upstairs, the chamber was a study in controlled chaos: books on art history lay open, sketches were pinned to a corkboard, and a half-finished sculpture sat on a stand, its clay still damp. On the dresser, beside a silver hip flask, lay a small, intricately carved wooden box. Davies opened it to find a collection of sculpting tools, their metal tips honed to a wicked sharpness, any one of which could have inflicted a similar wound to the one made by the letter opener.

Davies let the silence stretch for a moment, observing the reactions. Lady Eleanor flinched at Julian's crude words, while Dr. Finch remained placidly detached, polishing his spectacles with a silk handkerchief. Davies then turned his attention to Eleanor. "Lady Harrington, your husband's will... you mentioned it was a point of contention. Were there any recent changes you were aware of?" Her composure wavered for a fraction of a second. "Alistair was always threatening to change it. He used it as a tool, a weapon to control us all. He met with his solicitor only last week. I believe he intended to make Julian’s disinheritance official."

Leaving the drawing room's simmering tensions behind, Davies returned to the library. The crime scene technicians were meticulously dusting for prints, their quiet efficiency a balm to the inspector's frayed nerves. He walked over to the desk, his eyes scanning the surface. Lord Harrington's personal effects were arranged with military precision: a leather-bound blotter, an inkwell, a stack of unopened mail. His gaze fell upon a single sheet of paper, partially obscured by the blotter. It was a letter, penned in the victim's spidery handwriting, and it began with a stark, unforgiving phrase: "To my nephew, Julian, a final notice of your complete and utter disinheritance..."

Unfazed by the outburst, Davies redirected his attention to Lady Eleanor, whose composure remained impeccable, almost unnaturally so. "Lady Harrington, your husband's business… was it going well? Were there any recent pressures or concerns that he mentioned to you?" She delicately smoothed a non-existent wrinkle in her silk dress. "Alistair was always meticulous. The Harrington shipping line is a legacy, Inspector. It is… was… an empire. Of course, there are always rivals, but he never spoke of any specific threats. He kept his business affairs very private." Her words were precise, yet revealed nothing, like a beautifully crafted but empty porcelain vase.

The motive, it seemed, was now as clear as the crystal decanter on the sideboard. Davies envisioned the scene: the argument escalating, Lord Harrington brandishing the new codicil, Julian, in a fit of disinherited rage, snatching the nearest object—the silver letter opener—and plunging it into his uncle’s chest. The subsequent flight into the garden, leaving the muddy print, was the panicked act of a man who had just thrown away his future and his freedom in a single, fatal moment.
